```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

Petermann 2026 fitted two independent population PK models in MonolixSuite
2024R1 to therapeutic-drug-monitoring data from real-world patients with BRAF
V600E/K-mutant melanoma treated with the encorafenib + binimetinib combination.
Each drug is packaged as its own model; this article covers both.

* Encorafenib citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Petermann_2026_encorafenib"))$reference`
* Encorafenib description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Petermann_2026_encorafenib"))$description`
* Binimetinib description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Petermann_2026_binimetinib"))$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1007/s00280-026-04876-y> (open access, PMC13661740)

# Population

The encorafenib model was fitted to 310 concentrations from 66 patients and the
binimetinib model to 311 concentrations from 69 patients, followed at Cochin
University Hospital (Paris) and Ambroise Pare University Hospital
(Boulogne-Billancourt) between 2018 and 2024 (Petermann 2026 Table 1). Median
age was 62 years (IQR 52-71), median weight about 74 kg, and 32% (encorafenib)
or 29% (binimetinib) of patients were female. Hepatic function was normal or
mildly impaired. Encorafenib was given at a median 450 mg once daily (range
200-600 mg; 81% on 450 mg and 12% on 300 mg); binimetinib at 45 mg (81%) or
30 mg (19%) twice daily. Every sample was drawn at least 25 days after treatment
start or a dose change, so all data are at steady state, with a median of three
single-sample occasions per patient.

The same information is available programmatically via
`readModelDb("Petermann_2026_encorafenib")()$population` and
`readModelDb("Petermann_2026_binimetinib")()$population`.

# Source trace

Both models share one structure: a depot with first-order absorption into a
central compartment, linear elimination from central, and a peripheral
compartment exchanging with central through Q (Results, 'Population
pharmacokinetic model'; Methods, 'Base and covariate models'). No covariates
were retained.

| Parameter | Encorafenib | Binimetinib | Source location |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|-----------------|
| `lka` (ka, 1/h, held constant) | log(0.51) | log(0.76) | Results text; Table 2 prints the rounded 0.5 and 0.7 |
| `lcl` (CL/F, L/h) | log(29) | log(23) | Table 2 |
| `lvc` (Vc/F, L) | log(39) | log(35) | Table 2 |
| `lq` (Q/F, L/h) | log(1.7) | log(35) | Table 2 |
| `lvp` (Vp/F, L) | log(26) | log(106) | Table 2 |
| `etalcl` (variance) | 0.03189 (18 CV%) | 0.05155 (23 CV%) | Table 2; CV = sqrt(exp(omega^2) - 1) per Table 2 footnote |
| `etalvc` (variance) | 0.40819 (71 CV%) | not estimated | Table 2 |
| `etalq` (variance) | 0.61324 (92 CV%) | 1.34088 (168 CV%) | Table 2 |
| `propSd` | 0.44675 (47 CV%) | 0.43811 (46 CV%) | Table 2; same CV formula per Table 2 footnote |
| `Cc = 1000 * central / vc` | ng/mL | ng/mL | dose in mg, volume in L, concentrations reported in ng/mL |

# Virtual cohort and simulation

Three arms of 200 virtual patients each reproduce the Monte Carlo scenarios of
Figure 3: encorafenib 450 mg and 300 mg once daily, and binimetinib 45 mg twice
daily. Neither model has covariates, so the cohort needs no demographics.
Dosing runs for 21 days and the last dosing interval is sampled densely.
Concentrations are the individual predictions without residual error, as for
the paper's exposure metrics (Methods, 'Model-based bayesian predictions').

```{r cohort}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20260317)
n_per_arm <- 200

arms <- tibble::tribble(
  ~arm,                     ~drug,         ~dose, ~tau,
  "Encorafenib 450 mg QD",  "encorafenib", 450,   24,
  "Encorafenib 300 mg QD",  "encorafenib", 300,   24,
  "Binimetinib 45 mg BID",  "binimetinib", 45,    12
)
n_days <- 21

make_arm <- function(arm_row, n, id_offset) {
  tau <- arm_row$tau
  n_doses <- n_days * 24 / tau
  ss_start <- (n_doses - 1) * tau
  obs_t <- ss_start + sort(unique(c(seq(0, 4, by = 0.1), seq(4, tau, by = 0.5))))
  ids <- id_offset + seq_len(n)
  doses <- tidyr::expand_grid(id = ids, time = (seq_len(n_doses) - 1) * tau) |>
    dplyr::mutate(evid = 1L, amt = arm_row$dose, cmt = "depot")
  obs <- tidyr::expand_grid(id = ids, time = obs_t) |>
    dplyr::mutate(evid = 0L, amt = 0, cmt = "central")
  dplyr::bind_rows(doses, obs) |>
    dplyr::mutate(arm = arm_row$arm, ss_start = ss_start, tau = tau) |>
    dplyr::arrange(id, time, dplyr::desc(evid))
}

events <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(arms)), function(i) {
  make_arm(arms[i, ], n_per_arm, id_offset = (i - 1L) * n_per_arm)
}))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(unique(events[events$evid == 0, c("id", "time")])))

mod_enc <- readModelDb("Petermann_2026_encorafenib")
mod_bin <- readModelDb("Petermann_2026_binimetinib")

solve_arm <- function(mod, ev) {
  as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev, keep = c("arm", "ss_start", "tau"),
                                returnType = "data.frame"))
}
ev_enc <- dplyr::filter(events, grepl("Encorafenib", arm))
ev_bin <- dplyr::filter(events, grepl("Binimetinib", arm))
sim <- dplyr::bind_rows(solve_arm(mod_enc, ev_enc), solve_arm(mod_bin, ev_bin)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(tad = time - ss_start)
```

# Replicate Figure 3

```{r figure-3, fig.cap = "Steady-state concentration-time profiles over one dosing interval: median and 5th-95th percentile band of 200 simulated patients per arm. Replicates Figure 3 of Petermann 2026."}
sim |>
  dplyr::group_by(arm, tad) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    p05 = quantile(Cc, 0.05), p50 = median(Cc), p95 = quantile(Cc, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(tad, p50)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p05, ymax = p95), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~arm, scales = "free") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Time after dose (h)", y = "Concentration (ng/mL)") +
  theme_bw()
```

# PKNCA over the steady-state interval

```{r pknca}
nca_in <- sim |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, Cc, arm)

dose_df <- events |>
  dplyr::filter(evid == 1) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, amt, arm)

intervals <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(arms)), function(i) {
  ss_start <- (n_days * 24 / arms$tau[i] - 1) * arms$tau[i]
  data.frame(arm = arms$arm[i], start = ss_start, end = ss_start + arms$tau[i],
             auclast = TRUE, cmax = TRUE, cmin = TRUE, tmax = TRUE)
}))

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(nca_in, Cc ~ time | arm + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | arm + id)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))

nca_wide <- as.data.frame(nca_res) |>
  dplyr::select(arm, id, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES)
stopifnot(nrow(nca_wide) == nrow(arms) * n_per_arm)
```

## Internal identity: steady-state AUCtau equals Dose / CL

At steady state the AUC over one dosing interval equals `Dose / (CL/F)`
exactly. Both sides use each subject's own drawn clearance, so the difference
is trapezoidal error plus any residual approach to steady state, and a tight
bound is appropriate.

```{r identity}
indiv <- sim |>
  dplyr::distinct(id, arm, cl, vc, q, vp) |>
  dplyr::left_join(arms, by = "arm") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    kel = cl / vc, k12 = q / vc, k21 = q / vp,
    a = kel + k12 + k21,
    beta = 0.5 * (a - sqrt(a^2 - 4 * kel * k21)),
    thalf = log(2) / beta,
    auc_ref = 1000 * dose / cl
  )
ident <- nca_wide |>
  dplyr::left_join(indiv, by = c("arm", "id")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct = 100 * (auclast - auc_ref) / auc_ref)

ident |>
  dplyr::group_by(arm) |>
  dplyr::summarise(max_abs_pct = max(abs(pct)), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::rename("Arm" = arm, "Max absolute % difference" = max_abs_pct) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "PKNCA AUCtau vs the analytic Dose / CL.")
stopifnot(max(abs(ident$pct)) < 1)
```

## Comparison against Table 3

Table 3 reports the geometric mean of the Bayesian individual exposure metrics
of the real-world patients at standard dosing (median for Tmax). The simulated
summaries below use the same statistics; terminal half-life is computed from
each subject's micro-constants, as the paper does from its individual
parameters.

```{r compare-table3}
gmean <- function(x) exp(mean(log(x)))
sim_summary <- ident |>
  dplyr::filter(arm %in% c("Encorafenib 450 mg QD", "Binimetinib 45 mg BID")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(arm) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    cmin = gmean(cmin), cmax = gmean(cmax), auclast = gmean(auclast),
    tmax = median(tmax), half.life = gmean(thalf), .groups = "drop"
  )

published <- tibble::tribble(
  ~arm,                    ~cmin, ~cmax, ~auclast, ~tmax, ~half.life,
  "Encorafenib 450 mg QD", 18.6,  3378,  15785,    1.6,   12.5,
  "Binimetinib 45 mg BID", 55.0,  367,   2003,     1.1,   7.3
)

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = sim_summary,
  reference = published,
  by = "arm",
  units = c(cmin = "ng/mL", cmax = "ng/mL", auclast = "ng*h/mL",
            tmax = "h", half.life = "h"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(cmp, caption = paste(
  "Simulated (200 patients per arm) vs Petermann 2026 Table 3 real-life",
  "population. AUCtau is AUC0-24 for encorafenib and AUC0-12 for binimetinib.",
  "* differs from the reference by >20%."
))

auc_chk <- dplyr::inner_join(sim_summary, published, by = "arm",
                             suffix = c("_sim", "_pub"))
stopifnot(nrow(auc_chk) == 2)
auc_pct <- 100 * (auc_chk$auclast_sim - auc_chk$auclast_pub) / auc_chk$auclast_pub
# AUCtau depends only on dose and CL/F; a mis-transcribed CL or a missing
# ng/mL scaling moves it by tens of percent or orders of magnitude.
stopifnot(all(abs(auc_pct) < 10))
```

All five metrics of both drugs fall within 10% of the published values, with
no starred rows. AUCtau depends only on dose and CL/F and is asserted above;
Cmax, Cmin, Tmax and half-life also depend on the absorption and distribution
phases that the sparse data barely informed (ka was held constant for that
reason), and the published values are summaries of the real patients' Bayesian
estimates rather than of a Monte Carlo cohort, so they are shown without an
assertion.

## Unbound average concentration relative to IC50

Petermann 2026 computed the unbound average steady-state concentration as
`fu * AUCtau / tau`, with `fu` = 0.1390 (encorafenib) and 0.0280 (binimetinib),
and compared it with the IC50 values of 2.16 and 15.7 ng/mL (Methods, equation
for unbound Caverage; Results).

```{r unbound}
fu <- c(encorafenib = 0.1390, binimetinib = 0.0280)
ic50 <- c(encorafenib = 2.16, binimetinib = 15.7)
unbound <- ident |>
  dplyr::group_by(arm, drug, tau) |>
  dplyr::summarise(cavg = gmean(auclast / tau), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cavg_u = fu[drug] * cavg,
    ratio = cavg_u / ic50[drug],
    published_cavg_u = c(
      "Encorafenib 450 mg QD" = 89.7, "Encorafenib 300 mg QD" = 59.8,
      "Binimetinib 45 mg BID" = 4.67
    )[arm],
    pct_diff = 100 * (cavg_u - published_cavg_u) / published_cavg_u
  )
unbound |>
  dplyr::select(arm, cavg_u, ratio, published_cavg_u, pct_diff) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Arm" = arm, "Unbound Caverage (ng/mL)" = cavg_u,
    "Unbound Caverage / IC50" = ratio,
    "Published unbound Caverage (ng/mL)" = published_cavg_u,
    "% difference" = pct_diff
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = paste(
    "Geometric mean unbound Caverage of the simulated cohort. Encorafenib",
    "references are the Monte Carlo values in Results; the binimetinib reference",
    "is the value from the real patients' Bayesian estimates (see the deviations",
    "section for the published Monte Carlo value)."
  ))
stopifnot(all(abs(unbound$pct_diff) < 10))
```

# Assumptions and deviations

- **ka.** The Results text gives ka as 0.51 1/h (encorafenib) and 0.76 1/h
  (binimetinib); Table 2 prints the rounded values 0.5 and 0.7. The more precise
  text values are used.
- **Variance scale.** The Table 2 footnote states that the CV% of both the
  omegas and the proportional residual error was computed as
  `CV = sqrt(exp(omega^2) - 1)`. The variances are therefore
  `log(1 + CV^2)`. The same formula is applied to the residual error, giving
  `propSd = sqrt(log(1 + CV^2))` = 0.447 (encorafenib) and 0.438 (binimetinib).
  If instead the reported 47% and 46% were the raw Monolix proportional
  coefficients, `propSd` would be 0.47 and 0.46, about 5% higher; this changes
  only simulated observations with residual error, not the individual
  predictions used throughout this article.
- **No correlations.** Table 2 reports no covariances between random effects;
  the IIV is diagonal.
- **IIV on Vp, and on Vc for binimetinib.** Not estimated in the final models
  (Table 2 shows '/' for these rows); the corresponding parameters have no
  random effect.
- **Binimetinib Monte Carlo unbound Caverage.** The Results report a simulated
  geometric mean unbound Caverage of 11.4 ng/mL (ratio 0.75) for binimetinib
  45 mg twice daily. With `fu` = 0.0280 this would need an AUC0-12 near
  4,900 ng*h/mL, about 2.4 times the value implied by CL/F = 23 L/h
  (`45 / 23 * 1000` = 1,957 ng*h/mL) and the published real-life AUC0-12 of
  2,003 ng*h/mL; the real-life unbound Caverage of 4.67 ng/mL in the same
  paragraph is consistent with the model. The 11.4 ng/mL value cannot be
  reproduced from the published parameters, so the comparison uses 4.67 ng/mL.
  For encorafenib, the published Monte Carlo values (89.7 and 59.8 ng/mL, ratios
  41.5 and 27.7) are reproduced.
- **Residual error excluded** from every simulated metric, as in the paper's
  exposure-metric calculations.
- **Steady state** is approached by 21 days of dosing rather than an analytic
  steady-state solve; the AUC identity check above confirms the last interval
  is at steady state.
- No erratum or correction notice was found for this article in Europe PMC as of
  2026-11-18; the article's 13 October 2026 change-history note records only its
  move to open access.
